content: This can be calculated by subtracting the number of people aged 15 and older on ART from both the numerator (total population aged 15 and older with HIV) and the denominator (total population aged 15 and older) in national HIV prevalence estimates. Discrepant test results, also referred to as discordant results, occur when the outcomes of two or more HIV assays do not match. For instance, one assay may yield a reactive result while another shows a non-reactive result. Repeat testing involves retesting the same specimen using the same assay when the initial result is reactive or when test results are discordant. This process helps rule out biological false reactivity. For assays that use capillary whole blood, an additional finger prick may be required to collect enough specimen volume, but this must occur during the same testing event. Retesting refers to testing a second specimen from the same individual at a later time, following the same testing algorithm. This is not conducted during the same testing event. An HIV-inconclusive status is assigned when the testing strategy cannot definitively determine whether an individual is HIV-positive or HIV-negative. This is distinct from discrepant test results. Supplemental testing involves using additional assays or a set of assays to gather more information to ascertain HIV status. This is often employed to resolve inconclusive test results. Confirmatory testing uses specific assays to definitively confirm an initial reactive test result, providing a clear HIV-positive or HIV-negative status. While supplemental testing is sometimes incorrectly referred to as confirmatory testing, very few HIV assays can definitively rule out HIV infection (HIV-negative). HIV testing for diagnosis, including testing conducted for surveillance and surveys, can occur at all levels of the healthcare system. Ideally, HIV testing services (HTS) should be accessible at the first point of contact with the healthcare system, typically at the primary care level. Community-based HTS, including triage testing and self-testing, are crucial for reaching key populations and underserved groups, such as adolescent girls, young women, and men who may not visit healthcare facilities. The infrastructure required for each assay format determines the level of the healthcare system where testing can be conducted. For example, assays requiring reliable electricity and climate-controlled environments are unsuitable for lower-level facilities. The choice of assay format also depends on the availability of skilled staff. Assays with poor thermostability or those requiring invasive specimen collection (e.g., venepuncture) are not suitable for community or primary care levels. The programmatic use of an assay is as important as its sensitivity and specificity. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends using a testing strategy that combines rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) and/or enzyme immunoassays (EIAs) to achieve at least a 99% positive predictive value (PPV). In high HIV burden countries, three consecutive reactive test results are recommended to confirm an HIV-positive diagnosis. Countries with a national HIV prevalence above 5% may continue using two consecutive reactive tests but should monitor positivity rates and transition to three-test strategies as positivity rates decline. In Malawi, the number of adults living with HIV is projected to increase through 2025 due to longer lifespans on ART. However, the proportion of undiagnosed individuals has declined significantly, from 78% in 2005 to 14% in 2017, and is expected to drop further to 6% by 2025. This shift has led to a rapid decline in the proportion of HIV-positive test results and new HIV diagnoses. Despite a doubling in the number of people tested between 2015 and 2017, HIV testing positivity decreased by 50%, and new diagnoses have continued to decline since 2016. By 2025, the current two-test strategy in Malawi may result in a PPV below 97%, necessitating a shift to a three-test strategy. The WHO emphasizes the importance of retesting individuals diagnosed with HIV before initiating ART to catch human errors, such as mislabeling of test results. Retesting involves collecting and testing a new specimen using the same testing strategy but ideally at a different site or by a different provider with new test lots. For children under 18 months of age, serology assays alone are insufficient to confirm HIV infection due to the potential detection of maternal antibodies. Virological testing, typically using nucleic acid testing (NAT), is recommended for this age group. NAT technologies should not be used to rule out HIV infection in adults or children over 18 months of age who are on ART, as suppressed viral replication can lead to undetectable results. In summary, the WHO recommends a standardized HIV testing strategy using three consecutive reactive tests to confirm HIV-positive diagnoses, particularly in settings with declining positivity rates.
